title_original: How rebuilding old mosques is bringing Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims together in Punjab
editorial_title_zh: 重建老清真寺如何让旁遮普邦的锡克教徒、印度教徒和穆斯林走到一起
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在1947年印巴分治的宗派暴力期间，许多穆斯林的礼拜场所遭到毁坏或遗弃。如今，信仰各异的村民们正聚在一起重振这些场所。加朱·汗（Gajju Khan）坐在印度北部……的一处未完工的建筑里，面带微笑

article_text:
G ajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan , the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.

The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.

He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947 , he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.

“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”

Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.

“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”

During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two , unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.

But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.

About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.

Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.

“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”

For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.

“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.

“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.

Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib , or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.

Inspired by the former shahi , or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.

“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

title_original: 皮膚に刻まれた記憶と痛みを見つめる。黒沢艦人の写真展「new skins」が229 Gallery2で開催
editorial_title_zh: 凝视刻在皮肤上的记忆与痛苦。黑泽舰人摄影展“new skins”将在229 Gallery2举办
editorial_excerpt_zh: 摄影师黑泽舰人（Kanto Kurosawa）的个展“new skins”将于2026年10月12日（周一）至11月1日（周日）在东京新御徒町の229 Gallery2举办。以自身的身体与自画像为起点进行创作的“self”系列产
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影师黑泽舰人（Kanto Kurosawa）的个展“new skins”将于2026年10月12日（周一）至11月1日（周日）在东京新御徒町の229 Gallery2举办。展会将展出以自身的身体与自画像为起点进行创作的“self”系列中聚焦于“皮肤”的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此前，黑泽一直以自己的身体作为被拍摄主体，试图通过摄影将那些语言无法捕捉的感觉与感情可视化。其表现的核心，是将极度个人的身体经验转化为向他人开放的影像的行为。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展关注的“皮肤”既是隔绝身体内部与外界的边界，同时也是接触他人和世界的场所。此外，它也被视为内含过去经验、情感以及痛苦的场所。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对黑泽而言，痛苦不仅是单纯的身体刺激。它与塑造了自身的记忆和情感紧密相连，也是一种难以轻易语言化的内在经验。黑泽通过皮肤这一身体表面，将这种看不见的感觉转化成了摄影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "皮肤既是区分自我与他者的边界，同时也能成为连接两者的接触点。黑泽的摄影通过呈现个人的痛苦与记忆，试图唤起观者自身的身体感觉与经验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如展览标题“new skins”所示，本次展览是一次从重新审视身体表面出发，重新审视自我与他者关系的尝试。它通过摄影这一媒介，探索了无法言说的情感与他人共享的可能性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "标题", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "黑泽舰人“new skins”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "地点", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "229 Gallery2（东京都台东区台东4-24-2 2F）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "会期", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年10月12日（周一）〜11月1日（周日）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "时间", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "12:00〜19:00（周六、周日及节假日截至20:00）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "休息日", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "周二", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "费用", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1杯饮品点单制", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "URL", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "https://www.instagram.com/229.4242?obrf=MXJha2V6bjZmczhjeg%3D%3D&utm_source=qr", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为防止新冠病毒感染扩大，本网站刊载的展览及活动内容可能会有变更。请通过官方网站等确认最新信息。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
写真家・黒沢艦人（Kanto Kurosawa）の個展「new skins」が、2026年10月12日（月）から11月1日（日）まで、東京・新御徒町の229 Gallery2で開催される。自身の身体やセルフポートレートを起点に制作する「self」シリーズから、「皮膚」に焦点を当てた作品を発表する。

黒沢はこれまで、自身の身体を被写体としながら、言葉では捉えきれない感覚や感情を写真によって可視化することを試みてきた。その表現の中心にあるのは、極めて個人的な身体の経験を、他者にも開かれたイメージへと変換する行為だ。

本展で着目する「皮膚」は、身体の内側と外界を隔てる境界であると同時に、他者や世界と接触するための場所でもある。また、過去の経験や感情、痛みを内包する場所としても捉えられている。

黒沢にとって、痛みは単なる身体的な刺激ではない。それは自身を形づくってきた記憶や感情と深く結びついたものであり、容易に言語化することのできない内面の経験でもある。黒沢は皮膚という身体の表面を通して、そうした目に見えない感覚を写真へと置き換えていく。

皮膚は自己と他者を分かつ境界でありながら、同時に両者をつなぐ接点にもなり得る。黒沢の写真は、個人的な痛みや記憶を提示することで、鑑賞者自身の身体感覚や経験を呼び起こそうとするものだ。

展覧会タイトル「new skins」が示すように、本展は身体の表面を見つめ直すことから、自己と他者の関係を問い直す試みとなる。写真というメディアを介して、言葉にならない感情が他者と共有される可能性を探る。

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the end of an empty driveway, rain-slicked and littered with torn branches as though a storm had just passed, a white clapboard house comes into view. Light seeps from a single window, betraying a presence. The trees stand bare. The day promises little. Further into the book, a garage lies steeped in half-dark, where a cloud of smoke, the kind a tailpipe leaves behind, still hangs in the air."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jo Ann Chaus shows neither the man, nor the car, nor the leaving. She photographs the aftermath and hands the off-screen to the reader, who reassembles the missing scene alone. He has taken the motion with him; the stillness belongs to the one who stays, rendered invisible inside her own house. “The presence of absence is all pervasive,” notes Debra Klomp Ching, curator and co-owner of Klompching Gallery in New York, who writes the book’s foreword."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These two images dispel the misunderstanding at once. Unspoken is not about the 1950s but about their afterglow in the body of a woman who believed herself free of them. A modern professional, independent, unencumbered to all appearances, Jo Ann Chaus spent ten years arriving at the bitter opposite. “The photographs revealed my discomfort in finding myself internally imprisoned by these constraints,” she admits."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/11-chaus-rgb-684x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Jo Ann Chaus", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/05-chaus-rgb-684x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Jo Ann Chaus", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Born in Brooklyn in 1954, she grew up in Massapequa Park, on Long Island, in a Levitt tract house, the architecture that sheltered young postwar families and gave the American dream its floor plan, the same dream whose promises she now dismantles. “I was a child in the 1950s and a teenager in the 1960s,” she recalls. For many, that dream amounted to “just a façade.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Her mother, a devotee of the New Look that French couturier Christian Dior launched in 1947, trained her eye. Fabrics, colors, the arrangement of rooms: the whole interior bore her signature. At that very moment, “there was also an expectation that women would return to their dutiful positions as homemakers, a stark contrast to the emancipation women experienced as an essential workforce for the US war efforts.” The shadow of patriarchy was closing again over women who had kept the country running and drawn their own wages."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Before stepping behind the lens, Jo Ann Chaus put that schooling of the eye to work in women’s fashion retail, from 1978 to 1996. Seven years photographing her parents would follow. Sweetie & Hansom appeared in 2015, self-published. The project required her own image alongside theirs. “I was astounded to gaze into my own eyes; it was as if I was seeing myself for the very first time,” she says of that first self-portrait."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A gallery of characters follows: the maid, the debutante, the lady who lunches, the domestic housewife, the sex goddess, the sophisticate. Each session calls up a thrifted dress, jewelry, objects drawn from family closets. The artist works, she says, in “a dreamlike state of mental suspension,” and these garments return to her memories “of feelings, questions, and outlooks.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One more character haunts these pages: the house itself. article_text:
At the end of an empty driveway, rain-slicked and littered with torn branches as though a storm had just passed, a white clapboard house comes into view. Light seeps from a single window, betraying a presence. The trees stand bare. The day promises little. Further into the book, a garage lies steeped in half-dark, where a cloud of smoke, the kind a tailpipe leaves behind, still hangs in the air.

Jo Ann Chaus shows neither the man, nor the car, nor the leaving. She photographs the aftermath and hands the off-screen to the reader, who reassembles the missing scene alone. He has taken the motion with him; the stillness belongs to the one who stays, rendered invisible inside her own house. “The presence of absence is all pervasive,” notes Debra Klomp Ching, curator and co-owner of Klompching Gallery in New York, who writes the book’s foreword.

These two images dispel the misunderstanding at once. Unspoken is not about the 1950s but about their afterglow in the body of a woman who believed herself free of them. A modern professional, independent, unencumbered to all appearances, Jo Ann Chaus spent ten years arriving at the bitter opposite. “The photographs revealed my discomfort in finding myself internally imprisoned by these constraints,” she admits.

Born in Brooklyn in 1954, she grew up in Massapequa Park, on Long Island, in a Levitt tract house, the architecture that sheltered young postwar families and gave the American dream its floor plan, the same dream whose promises she now dismantles. “I was a child in the 1950s and a teenager in the 1960s,” she recalls. For many, that dream amounted to “just a façade.”

Her mother, a devotee of the New Look that French couturier Christian Dior launched in 1947, trained her eye. Fabrics, colors, the arrangement of rooms: the whole interior bore her signature. At that very moment, “there was also an expectation that women would return to their dutiful positions as homemakers, a stark contrast to the emancipation women experienced as an essential workforce for the US war efforts.” The shadow of patriarchy was closing again over women who had kept the country running and drawn their own wages.

Before stepping behind the lens, Jo Ann Chaus put that schooling of the eye to work in women’s fashion retail, from 1978 to 1996. Seven years photographing her parents would follow. Sweetie & Hansom appeared in 2015, self-published. The project required her own image alongside theirs. “I was astounded to gaze into my own eyes; it was as if I was seeing myself for the very first time,” she says of that first self-portrait.

A gallery of characters follows: the maid, the debutante, the lady who lunches, the domestic housewife, the sex goddess, the sophisticate. Each session calls up a thrifted dress, jewelry, objects drawn from family closets. The artist works, she says, in “a dreamlike state of mental suspension,” and these garments return to her memories “of feelings, questions, and outlooks.”

One more character haunts these pages: the house itself. Wood paneling, flowered wallpaper, framed canvases, shutters and curtains shut us inside a set where the world appears only through glass, more often than not fogged. An elegant prison, a deadening décor, whose residents grow numb. Debra Klomp Ching sees objects performing the role of vanitas, “not so much physical mortality, but rather the mortality of the spirit, the mind, emotions, and presence.”

Mustard yellows of damask wallpaper, moss greens of a tufted velvet, the faded roses of crumpled satin saturate the pages with an almost suffocating splendor. “Colors are lush and saturated, a conscious nod to the New Color Photography of the 1960s,” notes the American, who claims the lineage of William Eggleston and Saul Leiter, both faithful to Kodachrome, the reversal film Leiter shot past its expiration date to draw out those bleached, lavender-leaning tones.

Film that warm ought to warm whatever it records. Here it does the opposite. The brighter the golds, the harder the solitude sets; the more the satins blaze, the deeper the silence runs. Cold travels through color instead of resisting it, and sustaining that contradiction across seventy-two images owes as much to technical command as to the magic of the eye.

Light builds the narrative. “The lighting here is instrumental in conveying the internal momentum of change,” writes Jo Ann Chaus, who borrows film noir’s harshest contrasts. Her face withdraws without respite, hidden behind a hand mirror, dissolved in the condensation of a graffitied pane, shrunk to a miniature held captive in a reflection. Those mirrors speak, she says, “to the duality of my identity,” and they hand the power back to her. “One can’t look without the knowledge that Jo Ann Chaus is either looking right back or directing what the viewer is allowed to see,” Debra Klomp Ching warns.

Between these masks, flesh surfaces and resists. A bare back gives way across white sheets, bare feet cross a red floor, and in the green velvet of a cushion the hollow of a footprint remains. Objects take over from the body in “the oozing cake and dripping fluid that speaks to corporeality.” Sheer stockings dotted with black, lacquered nails, a cigarette whose smoke is savored for no one else: all betray a femininity that refuses to capitulate. No man ever enters the frame.

The body alone tells the weight of those years. “The postures, although strong and erect, in the earlier photographs depict a woman who looks confident, but something is awry. She seems to retreat into a position of powerlessness, as if waiting for permission,” the photographer observes. Then the shoulders loosen, the shoes come off, and the later images show her “having broken free from domestication, out and about, and being adventurous.”

Let us not mistake this for deliverance. A silhouette dwindles at the end of a path lined with gray sagebrush, in Idaho, where she seems to find her breath again. But Debra Klomp Ching tempers that “twilight of her journey” at once: the emergence “does in fact fall away through the continuum of equivocation, as evidenced in the subject’s stern expressions of melancholy and resignation.” Nothing guarantees the escape will hold.

It is impossible to move through these pages without thinking of the “Untitled Film Stills” Cindy Sherman made between 1977 and 1980. Where Sherman dissolved into anonymous cinematic archetypes, Jo Ann Chaus digs into her own bloodline and exposes a body that ages. A French reader may hear an echo of La Femme gelée , in which Annie Ernaux, the first Frenchwoman awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 2022, traced in 1981 the slow sinking of a brilliant young woman into housewifery, in the very years the photographer restages.

“There is no catharsis here, though. We turn the pages back and forth, back and forth,” the curator cautions. And yet a woman thaws, slowly, the way a window clears. The body, stiff at first inside its learned postures, eases, leans toward the door, readies its exit. It is the 1950s that dissolve in the end. Unspoken , a title of glacial restraint, cracks. Emancipation is never declared here. It is earned, one image at a time.

Unspoken by Jo Ann Chaus is published by Kehrer Verlag (2026), 152 pages, 72 color illustrations, hardcover, $58.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Pierson Fodé ( The Wrong Paris ) and comedian-actor Matteo Lane have joined Lucy Hale in the upcoming romantic fantasy feature Vision Board , which is due to shoot in New York from January.

Directed by Peter Hutchings, who reunites with Hale after The Hating Game and Which Brings Me to You , the Morgan Matson script “follows Emerson Mills (Hale), a struggling fashion designer whose life has fallen far short of her dreams. After a disastrous day, Emerson drunkenly creates a vision board, only to wake up in an alternate reality where everything she ever wanted has come true. Suddenly, she’s a wildly successful designer living in a Malibu mansion with a glamorous lifestyle. But as she navigates her new reality, she finds herself drawn to Jase (Fodé), a charming stranger who challenges her idea of happiness. Along the way, her older brother Henry (Lane), a bestselling author with an outsized personality, helps Emerson discover that getting everything you want isn’t always what you need.”

Related Stories

Sacha Gervasi Pic About Iron Maiden's Frontman In War-Torn Sarajevo Lands Scribe Arash Amel

Justin Long, Banks Pierce & Katy Mixon Greer Starring In Family Pic 'Slater's Gold'; Producer-Director Launches Texas Studio -- AFM

Claude Dal Farra and Brian Keady are producing through BCDF Pictures. Arlie Day & Mike Page are casting. Concourse Media is handling worldwide sales and will finance alongside newly launched Archetype Media Finance. Sales continue at this week’s AFM .

Watch on Deadline

“Reuniting with Lucy and Peter is a real pleasure, and Pierson and Matteo couldn’t be more perfect for the roles of Jase and Henry. Vision Board has everything we love about romantic comedies — humor, heart, and a little magic. Beneath the fantasy of getting everything you’ve ever wished for is a story we can all relate to: discovering that what makes us truly happy isn’t always what we thought we wanted,” stated producer Claude Dal Farra of BCDF Pictures.

Fodé recently starred opposite Miranda Cosgrove in Netflix’s romantic comedy The Wrong Paris and appears in Robert Zemeckis’ upcoming thriller The Last Mrs. Parrish , alongside Jennifer Lopez. His credits also include Swiped opposite Lily James.

Lane is a comedian and actor currently in the middle of his third international stand-up tour, We Gotta Catch Up . He has sold out venues including Radio City Music Hall, Chicago Theater and the Kennedy Center. This summer, he had his Broadway debut as Billy Flynn in Chicago . Previous credits include Abbott Elementary and Amazon’s Maintenance Required .

Fodé is repped by Range, CAA, and Gang, Tyre. Lane is repped by OPE Partners and Granderson Des Rochers.

article_text:
SoHo Project Space presents Slava Mogutin: NYC Go-Go 2.0 , an exhibition for the 20 th anniversary of the series.

In the early 2000s, Slava Mogutin began documenting New York’s go-go scene, taking pictures at The Cock and the now-defunct East Village bars Boysroom, Mr. Black, and Eastern Bloc, at a moment when downtown nightlife was already being ravaged by rising rents, gentrification, and increasing regulation.

“ NYC Go-Go was never intended as a project, social study, or critique. It was a straightforward documentary, shot from behind the scenes through relationships built on trust… Most of the men I photographed moved between odd jobs, dancing, sex work, and what is commonly referred to as ‘gay for pay,’” Mogutin writes in his artist statement . “I found that ambiguity intriguing. Class, race, and sexuality intersected with blurred boundaries between performance and reality, fantasy and livelihood. Desire, money, power, and survival could occupy the same space.”

The exhibition presents over 60 never-before-seen outtakes from Mogutin’s book NYC Go-Go , originally published by powerHouse Books. To accompany the exhibition, SoHo Project Space has published a limited-edition book with an essay by Bruce LaBruce.

“NYC Go-Go is Slava’s ode to that most noble and ridiculous of New York institutions, the go-go boy: sexual object, exhibitionist, narcissist, hustler, performance artist and working stiff (so to speak). It is pornography, portraiture, anthropology, nostalgia and social history all rolled into one sweaty, ample basket.” — Bruce LaBruce

Alongside NYC Go-Go , the Labor of Love exhibition offers a more intimate body of work documenting Mogutin’s relationship with Jesse Jordan. The photographs, also featured in the limited-edition book, form a vivid travelogue of their life together, moving between New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Berlin, London, and Mexico City. The series captures private moments, shared adventures, intimacy, and everyday life, offering a more personal counterpart to the communal energy and sexual charge of NYC Go-Go . The book also features Mogutin’s handwritten poetry and text drawings. Together, the two bodies of work span two decades of Mogutin’s photography, moving from the nightlife underground to the private space from distinctly different perspectives.

Born in Siberia, Slava Mogutin was exiled from Russia for his outspoken queer writing and activism. A third-generation writer and self-taught photographer, he is the first Russian to be granted political asylum in the US on the grounds of homophobic persecution. For the past three decades, he has documented queer communities around the world. Informed by his bicultural experience as a dissident and refugee, Mogutin’s work explores displacement and identity, pride and shame, devotion and disaffection, love and hate. He is the author of numerous books, artist editions, and zines, and a recipient of the Andrei Bely Prize for Poetry and the Tom of Finland Foundation Award for Artistic Achievement.

SoHo Project Space 127-B Prince Street NYC 10012 www.sohoprojectspace.com www.nycgogo.com

article_text:
Tree Week: Jamie V. Robertson: In Search of Osman’s Ghost

©Jamie V. Robertson, Osman in the Swamp Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2024

I met Jamie V. Robertson at the FotoFest reviews in Houston, and was immediately struck by the quiet strength of her images of southern swamplands. The pictures are taken with Infrared film, which makes the tree foliage seem luminescent. This haunting effect is tied into her exploration of the maroon colonies of runaway slaves that lived deep in the swamp. The farther in the escapees went, the less likely it was that the slave catchers would follow you. Robertson skillfully adds historical drawings of runaways to her images to help the viewer visualize the terror those people felt.

©Jamie V. Robertson,Spirited Away Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2024

In Search of Osman’s Ghost

In Search of Osman’s Ghost is a photographic series that explores the connection between humanity and nature by illuminating maroonage in the Southern Swamplands. Informed by the literary works of Toni Morrison, bell hooks, Lucille Clifton, and Édouard Glissant, the Southern Swamp is reframed as a living collaborator for runaway slaves in colonial America. Its ‘rememory’ of maroons, self-liberated formerly enslaved people who lived on the fringes of colonial America, is explored through black and white infrared photography and archival illustrations. Infrared film, which has applications in science, medicine, and paranormal studies, captures images outside of the visible light spectrum, giving a surreal and otherworldly experience of the environment. Can a swamp dream? What or who does it dream of? Does it remember its brief alliance with those seeking freedom? The surrealist nature of infrared images allows for the exploration of memory in the landscape. The Great Dismal Swamp in Virginia, the Everglades in Florida, and the Bas Du Fleuve of New Orleans were sites of maroonage where Africans and African Americans made their dream of freedom a reality. This series looks at the Swamp, the maroons, and how their alliance defied colonial standards of living. In Search of Osman’s Ghost invites the viewer to explore this counternarrative of America’s history to consider their own relationship to the natural world.

©Jamie V. Robertson, A Place To Steal Oneself Away II Inkjet Print 72 x 46 inches 2025

Jamie V. Robertson (B. 1988 American) is a visual artist and educator working in photography and video. Born and raised in Houston, her Texas roots inform her practice as she examines the environment of the American South and its relationship to Black counter-narratives. Through research, writing, photography, and video art, her work excavates a history of Black defiance, contending with the vilified and monolithic narrative of the Southern United States. Deeply influenced by the works of Toni Morrison, bell hooks, and Lucile Clifton, her creative practice embraces a Black Feminist Hauntology, a framework that acknowledges the spectral presence in Southern land through untold histories. Her approach to image-making fluidly oscillates between analog and digital processes, with an emphasis on black and white infrared film. Robertson utilizes text, archival images, and found imagery as materials and companions to her work to oppose the hierarchy of high and low culture.

Jamie earned an MFA in Studio Art from the University of Houston and an MS in Art Therapy from Florida State University. Robertson is an Assistant Professor at Old Dominion University and works between Texas and Virginia. Currently, her research explores the Great Dismal Swamp and maroonage.

©Jamie V. Robertson, The Runaway Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2024

Can you tell me what drew you to photograph this project, and how you felt when you were doing it.

I have always had an interest in the natural world and its intersection with Black History. My early work dealt with my family’s history and relationship to the Texas Freedom Colony, Egypt Community, outside of Centerville, TX. My family has held land there since emancipation. The term “Freedom Colony” comes from the work of Dr. Andrea Roberts at UVA. In hindsight the move into marronage in North America feels like a natural shift. There is a lot of overlap between maroon colonies and freedom colonies. I have always known about maroons in other parts of the Americas like Jamaica, Brazil and Colombia but I had never heard them mentioned in the United States. It was a podcast episode with historian Marcus Nevis, on his book, City of Refuge, that really piqued my interest. As I began to do more research I became excited by this history of rebellion and resistance.

©Jamie V. Robertson, A Place To Steal Oneself Away III Inkjet Print 72 x 46 inches 2025

Who was Osman, and was he a real person who was related to you?

This series is a move away from my family history work and the beginnings of looking at collective histories. Osman was a real person who lived in the Great Dismal Swamp. The only details we have of him come from David Hunter Strother in 1856 who was traveling through the swamp after a visit to an enslaved workers’ camp. He sees Osman briefly in the thicket of the swamp armed with a rifle. And just like a figment of the imagination, he was gone. Osman was a maroon but colonial society would have probably referred to him as a fugitive or runaway. Maroons were people who ran away from slavery and built autonomous communities in the hinterlands. In Jamaica, they lived in the mountains, in the U.S. , the Swamp was the primary location. These communities were difficult for colonial authorities to reach on purpose. Outside New Orleans, which I am hoping to photograph in the near future, St. Jean Malo, a maroon leader, had signs posted with warnings informing trespassers they were entering maroon territory.

©Jamie V. Robertson, Kudzu and Clouds Archival Inkjet Print 18 x 24 inches 2025

How did you first find out about the maroon people and the slaves who escaped to freedom in the swamps?

I’m not really sure when I first learned of maroons. I knew Black enclaves of resistance existed throughout the Americas. However, these were things I learned outside of the academic environment. The nuance of the lives of Black people during slavery is always missing from K-12 education. For instance, the lives of enslaved people in cities like Norfolk and New Orleans were very different from those who were enslaved on the plantations in the Sea Islands. Enslaved people in cities worked in various trades and often moved about the city unsupervised versus those who worked in the fields were under constant surveillance by an overseer.That specificity is worth noting. Maroonage is a byproduct of the system of slavery and essential to understanding that time period as well as the fact that Black people resisted slavery.

©Jamie V. Robertson, An Obscure Place To Hide 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2024

It must have been very difficult living conditions, with constant fear of being captured. Do you know what happened to them?

The swamp absolutely has its dangers. In the Life of Moses Grandy, he talks about escaping to the Great Dismal Swamp. One night while sleeping he felt the wet nose of some animal sniffing him. Moses eventually escaped North and was more or less passing through the swamp. Historians called this Petit Marronage because people’s stay was short term. As for the people who really lived there, we really don’t know what they thought of the environment other than it was a fantastic place to hide because all these dangers protected them from slave catchers who really didn’t want to venture deep into that terrain. One historian, Ryne Beddard, suggests that some of the first Africans who escaped into the swamp more than likely saw it as a sacred place because of their own cultural cosmologies. I like this reading the best because we tend to think about history from our position in the present and this reading honors what would have been the interior culture of enslaved people. As for what happened to maroons, it varies. In Jamaica , they still live in the mountains until this day. As for the United States, I would imagine that some mixed in with various indigenous people and maybe others came out of the swamp after emancipation.

©Jamie V. Robertson, Beware the Hounds 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2026

How do your images allude to the people and natural environment?

My series, In Search of Osman’s Ghost, uses black and white infrared photographs of southern swamplands and archival illustrations of maroons, runaways and resistance leaders to make visible the historic alliance between Black Americans and the natural world. Infrared film, which has applications in science, medicine, and paranormal studies, captures images outside of the visible light spectrum, giving a surreal and otherworldly experience of the environment. My process is two-fold. I spend time photographing historic wetland environments with black and white infrared film. As of late, I have started looking at expired rolls of films like Efke IR 820 and Macophot because they go deeper into the electromagnetic spectrum than the newer stocks. The images can range from soft to sharp depending on the brand and film size.The second part involves researching digital archives for images of maroons, runaways and fugitives. Maroons materialize in these images through the use of Photoshop. Conceptually, I have begun to think about these images as surreal. D. Scot Miller’s 2009 manifesto titled, ‘Call it Afro-Surreal’ really resonated with me. He states,“Afro-Surreal presupposes that beyond this visible world, there is an invisible world striving to manifest, and it is our job to uncover it. Like the African Surrealists, Afro-Surrealists recognize that nature (including human nature) generates more surreal experiences than any other process could hope to produce.”These sentiments along with the writings of Toni Morrison and bell hooks inform my framework of living memory in the landscape.

©Jamie V. Robertson, An Obscure Place To Hide II 18 x 24 inches Archival Inkjet Print 2026

I’d like to know what it was like to work in the swamp? Did you have issues with your equipment? Did you photograph from a boat or from the shore?

I really enjoy being out in the swamp. I photograph primarily in Virginia, Texas and Louisiana. I’m hoping to hit more Southern states in the coming years. In spite of the general term, ‘swamp’, they all feel different. The Great Dismal Swamp is very still and there are parts that don’t feel much like a traditional swamp at all. In Texas, I primarily focus on the bayous. In Houston alone the bayous range from heavily polluted ( like the one I grew up by) to wild. I often make my photographs from the shoreline or the side of the road. Sometimes, I lower my POV to imply being on the water. But also wetlands are low-lying areas. Some of the best things are happening pretty low to the ground. I haven’t had many issues with equipment other than an shutter release breaking or wishing that I had brought more film. As for wildlife, I have yet to see a snake, alligator or bear (knock on wood) but there are lots of insects, turtles and aquatic mammals like otters.The mosquitos can be brutal so I always carry insect repellent. I don’t feel afraid being out there even when I am alone because a lot of my experience is mediated by being on trails or walking over a cypress swamp via a boardwalk. It’s not hard to use your imagination about how the place would look without so much human intervention.

article_text:
ジェームズ・ディーンにさよならを

劇場公開日： 2026年10月16日

解説・あらすじ

名優ジェームズ・ディーンの突然の死に直面した若者たちを主人公に、彼らの運命を変えた1日の出来事を鮮烈に描いた青春映画。「ペーパーチェイス」「チャイナ・シンドローム」のジェームズ・ブリッジス監督が、自身の故郷アーカンソー州を舞台に自らの青春時代を投影して撮りあげた。 1955年9月30日、若き映画俳優ジェームズ・ディーンが自動車事故で急逝した。ディーンを崇拝する大学生ジミー・Jは、激しい喪失感に打ちのめされてしまう。悲嘆のあまり自暴自棄に陥った彼は、戸惑う恋人や学友も巻き込みながら、酒を飲み、車を飛ばし、同じくディーン信者の少女ビリー・ジーンと共に私的な追悼会を開こうとする。歯止めの効かない奇妙な一夜は、彼らのその後の人生を一変させることになる。 テレビドラマ「わが家は11人」のリチャード・トーマスが主演を務め、「ゴングなき戦い」のスーザン・ティレル、「愛と青春の旅だち」のリサ・ブロント、キャリア初期のデニス・クエイドが共演。「ゴッドファーザー」シリーズのゴードン・ウィリスが撮影を手がけ、ジェームズ・ディーン主演作「エデンの東」のレナード・ローゼンマンが音楽を担当。日本ではテレビ放送されたのみで長らく劇場未公開のままだったが、上映企画「CULT CLASSICS（カルト・クラシックス）」の第1弾作品として2026年10月に劇場初公開。

article_text:
Filme chega aos cinemas em 11 de fevereiro.

A Netflix divulgou o trailer de “ Nárnia: O Sobrinho do Mago “, novo filme de Greta Gerwig e um dos mais aguardados do ano. Assista acima (dublado).

Foi divulgado também o primeiro cartaz oficial do filme, abaixo.

O filme é uma releitura moderna do primeiro livro da série “As Crônicas de Nárnia”, de C.S. Lewis. A história acompanha os novos amigos Polly Plummer (Beatrice Campbell) e Digory Kirke (David McKenna), que descobrem que o tio de Digory, Andrew Ketterley (Daniel Craig), pode ser louco o suficiente para ter arquitetado uma maneira de transitar entre mundos infinitos.

Além de Campbell, McKenna e Craig, o elenco conta ainda com Carey Mulligan, Kobna Holdbrook-Smith, Denise Gough, Susan Wokoma e Meryl Streep. Direção e roteiro são de Greta Gerwig.

article_text:
写真家パスカル・グレコによるトークイベントが、渋谷の404 Not Foundにて開催される。グレコは、ビデオゲーム内の仮想空間を写真として捉える「インゲームフォトグラフィー」に取り組んできた写真家。建築や都市、風景を撮影してきたこれまでの視点をゲーム空間に持ち込み、仮想世界のイメージと現実の風景写真、記憶との関係を問い続けている。

本トークイベントは、9月25日から10月4日まで同会場で開催される写真・映像展「PHOTOGRAPHING THE VIRTUAL IN THE AGE OF ANIMA LUDENS」にあわせて企画されたもの。会期中の10月2日には、写真家の小林健太に、編集者、クリエイティブディレクター、アートプロデューサーの後藤繁雄を迎え、グレコを交えた三者によるトークを行う。デジタル環境のなかで「写真を撮る」とはどのような行為なのか。グレコの実践を写真史・現代写真の文脈から読み解き、現実と仮想空間を横断する今日の写真の可能性を考える機会となる。

なお本展では、グレコがビデオゲームの風景を撮影した写真シリーズ「Photography, Video Game, Landscape」に連なる作品と映像作品を紹介する。ぜひ会場に足をお運びいただきたい。

場所

404 Not Found（東京都渋谷区桜丘町1-4 Shibuya Sakura Stage SHIBUYA SIDE 4F）

日程

2026年10月2日（金）

時間

18:30〜20:00

URL

https://www.arsobit.com/pascal-greco-404-exhibition/

Last year, “Sinners” DP Autumn Durald Arkapaw, “KPop Demon Hunters” songwriter EJAE and “One Battle After Another” editor Andy Jurgensen all went on to win Oscars."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Anne Jimkes Supervising sound editor, “The Mosquito Bowl” Jimkes approached the film’s World War II Pacific Theater setting with a focus on authenticity, researching the specific weapons used by the Japanese and American military forces, including the M1 Garand rifle. Its distinctive metallic “ping” served as more than just a historically accurate reference. “It adds a sense of urgency, and it’s a decision-making moment,” Jimkes says, noting the sound signals when a character must reload, switch weapons or resort to hand-to-hand combat. The sounds of the soldiers were a priority. The breaths and physical reactions recorded on set were pushed forward against the chaos of the battle to ground the characters’ humanity. Even in quieter scenes, the jungle location was alive with sound, creating a sense of pressure surrounding the soldiers. Blending these elements together is a process Jimkes refers to as a “parade of sound,” adding, “Your brain can only process so many sounds at the same time. However, it’s very good at processing rapidly successive sounds.” The sound needed to move the story forward. For Jimkes, that meant determining which sound should take priority in each moment while never losing sight of the people at the center of the film’s story. — Tanya Fedak"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Anne-Jimkes-Root.jpg?w=240", "alt": "Anne Jimkes", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Aulo Licinio Image Credit: Credit: Felix Guenette Animation supervisor, “Project Hail Mary” Despite having no face, eyes or traditional way to convey human emotion, Rocky became the emotional heart of “Project Hail Mary.” Licinio navigated that by developing physical language for the alien rock creature. Licinio oversaw a team of animators who studied the physical puppet used for filming, using its on-set movements as a reference while expanding Rocky’s mannerisms. “[Rocky’s puppeteer and voice] James Ortiz did a good job getting expressions out of this rock,” he says. “How can we enhance it in a way that we can use in reference? article_text:
In 2026, moviegoers came back to cinemas, packing theaters to see blockbusters like “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Toy Story 5,” “Michael” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and low-budget films like “Backrooms” and “Obsession.” But all those movies needed skilled artisans to complete the directors’ visions, including those on Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch list. The honorees will be feted at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, which runs Oct. 24-31.

Past honorees have often gone on to earn Oscar nominations. Last year, “Sinners” DP Autumn Durald Arkapaw, “KPop Demon Hunters” songwriter EJAE and “One Battle After Another” editor Andy Jurgensen all went on to win Oscars.

Anne Jimkes Supervising sound editor, “The Mosquito Bowl” Jimkes approached the film’s World War II Pacific Theater setting with a focus on authenticity, researching the specific weapons used by the Japanese and American military forces, including the M1 Garand rifle. Its distinctive metallic “ping” served as more than just a historically accurate reference. “It adds a sense of urgency, and it’s a decision-making moment,” Jimkes says, noting the sound signals when a character must reload, switch weapons or resort to hand-to-hand combat. The sounds of the soldiers were a priority. The breaths and physical reactions recorded on set were pushed forward against the chaos of the battle to ground the characters’ humanity. Even in quieter scenes, the jungle location was alive with sound, creating a sense of pressure surrounding the soldiers. Blending these elements together is a process Jimkes refers to as a “parade of sound,” adding, “Your brain can only process so many sounds at the same time. However, it’s very good at processing rapidly successive sounds.” The sound needed to move the story forward. For Jimkes, that meant determining which sound should take priority in each moment while never losing sight of the people at the center of the film’s story. — Tanya Fedak

Aulo Licinio Image Credit: Credit: Felix Guenette Animation supervisor, “Project Hail Mary” Despite having no face, eyes or traditional way to convey human emotion, Rocky became the emotional heart of “Project Hail Mary.” Licinio navigated that by developing physical language for the alien rock creature. Licinio oversaw a team of animators who studied the physical puppet used for filming, using its on-set movements as a reference while expanding Rocky’s mannerisms. “[Rocky’s puppeteer and voice] James Ortiz did a good job getting expressions out of this rock,” he says. “How can we enhance it in a way that we can use in reference? How can we tie the loose ends?” Licinio and his team looked to early puppetry and the exaggerated performances from silent film stars like Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton. Without features to convey human emotion, Rocky instead uses his elbows, body and distinctive head movements, sometimes angling himself just five degrees more to express his feelings. When he is shy, for example, he pulls an elbow in front of himself as if hiding. Some of Rocky’s mannerisms originated on set, including a tapping gesture to answer questions from Ortiz that the animators incorporated into the final character. Other movements, such as Rocky’s finger-like computing gestures, were created in CG. “It’s a collaboration at the end,” Licinio says. “That’s what I like to say about the film.” — T.F.

Landon Lott Art director, Concept Illustrator, “Pluribus” SCAD alum Lott recalls “Pluribus” production designer Denise Pizzini reaching out to help develop a Norwegian ice hotel that would be built entirely on stage. Lott recalls, “The brief was to create a hotel that felt authentic and entirely sculpted from ice, while designing it around the practical limitations of a stage build.” Lott, who worked as a concept illustrator on the show, saw it as a great opportunity to bring together his background in illustration, architecture and set design. On his process, Lott says, “The initial scope of the set was actually larger than what ultimately appeared on screen and included a hotel lobby, foyer, bar and the individual hotel rooms. That meant thinking through the hotel as a complete environment from the beginning, establishing how the spaces connected and giving each one its own identity while making sure they all felt like part of the same place.” Lott knew that many details would be handcarved by ice sculptors. “I was essentially designing artwork that also had to function architecturally, work within the realities of a stage build and give the sculptors something tangible they could interpret and bring to life,” he says. So he turned to real ice hotels throughout Scandinavia, particularly the ICEHOTEL in Sweden and hotels in Norway and Finland for inspiration. — Jazz Tangcay

Blair McClendon Editor, “Clarissa” For McClendon, editing films is a lot like music. It’s all about finding the right rhythm, texture, pace and cutting where the beat falls. Sometimes finding this groove is deliberate and difficult, and other times, like on “Clarissa,” the experience is filled with happy accidents. “It’s like a rooster crows at exactly the right moment to keep the shot interesting and keep it going, and we were like, ‘Oh, that’s great, that guy has to stay,’” McClendon says. It also helped that the actors delivered great performances, McClendon explains. Stars David Oyelowo, Sophie Okonedo and Ayo Edebiri worked with directors Arie Esiri and Chuko Esiri to allow scenes to unfurl naturally and used editing to enhance characters’ emotions. To achieve a final cut, McClendon and the directors discussed their wishes and ideas for what the film would be, and McClendon aimed to make as many of them come true as possible. He knew he was done when they had “emotionally exhausted the avenues of what you’re trying to make.” By the end, he could happily accept that “this is the movie this movie is. It’s not the movie that is in my head or Chuko’s head or Arie’s head or the producer’s head or the DP’s head, but you start to recognize, like, no, that is how this movie runs,” McClendon says. — Isabelle Farina

Adam Newport-Berra Image Credit: Variety via Getty Images Cinematographer, “The Invite”, “Club Kid” Newport-Berra’s range is on display in two films this awards season: “The Invite,” directed by and starring Olivia Wilde, and “Club Kid,” directed by and starring Jordan Firstman. “I tend to enjoy working with actor-directors because we get this dynamic experience on set where they get to direct the film both from outside and from within during the scene, which I think is a special opportunity for a director to be inside the moment,” Newport-Berra says. “The Invite” takes place over one night and follows two dynamic couples inside one apartment. The premise provided Wilde and Newport-Berra with a creative challenge. “We loved the script, but we thought, ‘How do we make this really sing on screen?’ It can’t just feel like a play. It can’t just be about presenting the material. It needs to be dynamic.” Newport-Berra sought ways to liberate his camera within the confines of the space. With no big cranes available, lensing and composition had to tell the story. “Olivia and I looked through a lot of references, took a lot of photos and talked about why certain images make us feel awkward, seduced, anxious or in love,” he explains. “We really used composition and the focal lengths of our lenses to either compress people and make things feel flat and claustrophobic, or we would use a wider lens to make it feel very intimate, gentle, sexy and seductive.” “Club Kid” emphasizes the character dynamics. Firstman’s Peter finds his life turned upside down after years of partying in New York clubs when he learns he has a 10-year-old son, Arlo (Reggie Absolom). Newport-Berra wanted to handle the relationship between Reggie and Jordan’s characters with care. “It was through rehearsals, and every morning, Jordan and I would check in, read through the script together, and feel whatever we were feeling that day,” Newport-Berra says. — J.T.

Raül Refree Composer, “La Bola Negra” When scoring Netflix’s “La Bola Negra,” Refree knew he wanted to pursue a timeless, orchestral and avant-garde sound. The film recounts the story of three generations of queer men whose lives are connected through love and loss. Refree tied his instrumentation to the characters rather than the eras. “Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) plays the trumpet, so his scenes rely heavily on the brass section. Carlos (Milo Quifes) plays the piano, so his music features the piano alongside the string section. Finally, Alberto’s (Carlos González) story takes place in the present day, and because he is going through a personal crisis, his music relies much more on silence,” Refree says. The film contains several songs including “La Nieve,” sung by Sebastián. “Guitarricadelafuente brought the idea for ‘La Nieve’ to Los Javis (the film’s directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo). They loved it and asked me to incorporate it into the score, so I adapted his initial concept to align with the rest of the soundtrack,” Refree says. “Having worked with Guitarricadelafuente frequently over the last few years, we have a great creative dynamic, which made it easy to co-write the song and develop the right sound.” — J.T.

Jessica Ronane Image Credit: Yellow Belly Photo Casting director, “Elsinore” Casting for “Elsinore” was a particularly nuanced feat for Ronane. She felt a responsibility to the truth. She had to cast a play within a film based on the real-life happenings of London’s National Theatre in 1989. To do so, Ronane and “Elsinore” director Simon Stone worked closely together scouring their web of actors and building a “story map of all the real people and then started to think about instinctively who has the spirit of the character, and how are we going to identify the right actors to put forward,” Ronane says. Ronane’s instincts led her to focus on performers with theater experience. Once Andrew Scott was solidified for the role of Ian Charleson, Ronane quickly thought of David Dawson to play Derek Jarman. She had seen the pair perform together in a play back in 2014 and couldn’t shake their chemistry. “Seeing the two of them on a small stage together like that in a really intimate setting, I could not stop thinking about that when we spoke about David Dawson in this role,” Ronane says. Casting Olivia Colman as Margaret was also instinctual. Her “particular brand of sensitivity and humor and wisdom and sort of spiciness” made her a natural choice to play the part, Ronane says. “What an incredible thing to be able to build on your instincts like that, to be able to really feel that your taste is appreciated by collaborators who want kind of more of that,” Ronane says. — I. F.

Allie Shehorn Make-up and hair department head/ special makeup effects department head, “Obsession” For “Obsession,” Shehorn was tasked with creating looks that could withstand the film’s practical effects while still telling the characters’ stories. For Sarah’s (Megan Lawless) face-smash sequence, Shehorn crafted multiple versions of the character’s head, including a live cast taken from the actor as she screamed and a prosthetic version that could ultimately be smashed on camera. Shehorn and the team carefully choreographed each transition, switching from the actor’s live-action performance to the prosthetic before revealing Sarah’s final smashed-in face. Working with the blood rigs presented another technical challenge, particularly because the team filmed scenes out of order. “We actually shot the end sequence of the movie before we did the blood rigs to establish the blood looks,” Shehorn says. “We had to predict where the blood was going on Bear (Michael Johnston), even on Nikki (Inde Navarrette).” One of Shehorn’s more elaborate looks was Nikki’s final appearance after murdering Sarah, which reflects her growing obsession with becoming her. Shehorn used the same lipstick and eyeliner shades on Nikki that Sarah wears, while dried blood sits beneath the fresh blood to represent the fact that Nikki never washes it from her face. She also used Sarah’s eyeliner shade to draw Nikki’s tattoos and, by the end of the film, curled Nikki’s hair as another visual connection to Sarah. “That’s why we kept Nikki’s hair straight throughout the film, because we wanted to show the difference in the characters between Sarah and Nikki, so that in the end we can really push those moments of ‘Oh, she’s really trying to be her,’” she says. — T.F.

Grace Snell Costume designer, “Sense and Sensibility” Snell is a Jane Austen fan, but she tried not to be intimidated by the fact that “Sense and Sensibility” was an Austen adaptation. “I took my role very seriously and did lots of research, but then I was reassured by our director and the producers that they wanted my version of this,” she says. “What I wanted to do was design a film that I could see myself in, see my friends in, see my family in, try and knock down the wall that often is associated with period dramas.” Georgia Oakley’s film isn’t the first “Sense and Sensibility” adaptation, and while Snell loves the 1995 version, she also knew this film was a different take. Part of that was her blend of modern styling and historical accuracy. “As a designer, it was an amazing experience to try and fight those two sides,” she says. With help from a dress historian, Snell created a modern take on costumes from the “tip of Regency” era using historically accurate fabrics and hand-sewing techniques. Snell was also inspired by family portraits. She wanted the Dashwood women to share clothing in the way that sisters do. “The dynamic of those sisters and how they share clothes and how they’re inspired by each other was important,” she says. “We do rework some of the fabrics so that the garments look like they have a life themselves and how garments are loved and shared and borrowed within a family.” — Mya Copeland

Danny Vermette Production designer, “Backrooms” Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” web series became a YouTube phenomenon, amassing over 200 million views across its episodes. When Parsons began adapting the series into a feature film, Vermette had already seen the series but wasn’t fully aware of Parsons’ work. “I watched all of Kane’s stuff and came to realize how much is out there, and what a following it had,” Vermette says. He jokingly refers to this experience as attending “Backrooms University.” In conversations with Parsons, Vermette realized there was much more to the concept than just liminal spaces. Bringing the world to life as a period piece — the story is set in the 1990s — required close collaboration with the film’s cinematographer Jeremy Cox and costume designer Micah Cade to determine what would work within “the yellow universe.” One of the challenges was designing the drop ceilings. “My key thought was to keep this original to the series but bring it up to that next level of cinema and make it beautiful,” Vermette explains. The ceilings were customized, which turned into a major undertaking. “There were a lot, a lot of lights — 375 individual lenses and troffers on the set.” Finding multiples of the same furniture became a challenge. Lead buyer Eric Cairns was tasked with finding 32 of the exact same couches in the tone they wanted. Parsons questioned it. article_text:
In this episode, we look back at the story of Aina, an organisation set up to train a new generation of Afghan journalists, photographers and documentary-makers, so that Afghanistan can tell its own story through its own media. These initiatives are carried out with a particular focus on the Afghan women being trained.

Reza, co-founder of Aina, shares his experiences on the ground in Afghanistan.

He recounts meeting a young boy proudly holding a small plant in his hands, which for him has become a symbol of a possible future.

Rachel Deghati, co-founder of Aina, reflects on the organisation’s work, the efforts to pass on knowledge and the challenges encountered. She also pays tribute to those humanitarian workers from around the world who, within Aina, worked collaboratively with Afghan women and men to create spaces for freedom and reconstruction.

article_text:
While Quentin Tarantino is doing everything possible not to direct his tenth and potentially final film (including prepping the new stage play The Popinjay Cavaliers , a 1830s Europe-set swashbuckling comedy starring Sacha Baron Cohen), his latest contribution to cinema will come via his script for David Fincher’s newly titled The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , a continuation of Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood centered on Brad Pitt’s character.

With a two-week IMAX engagement (for which Netflix will actually report the grosses) set for November 25, before debuting on the streaming platform on December 24, there’s a new trailer that finally begins to reveal the contours of Tarantino’s plot, which has been compared (seemingly not-inaccurately) to an Elmore Leonard paperback.

Here’s the very brief synopsis from Netflix: “Brad Pitt returns to his Academy Award-winning role as Cliff Booth, only this time it’s 1977 and it’s a very different Hollywood. Directed by David Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino, the film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis, and Karren Karagulian, and will be produced by Pitt and Ceán Chaffin.”

In addition to Pitt and Chaffin, the film’s creative team includes Erik Messerschmidt, ASC, as director of photography, and Donald Graham Burt as production designer. It’s edited by Kirk Baxter, ACE, with casting by Laray Mayfield. Trish Summerville is costume designer, Ren Klyce is sound designer, and Dave Macomber is stunt coordinator.

article_text:
山上に広がる総石垣の城

羽柴秀吉は関白に任官した天正 13 年（ 1585 ）閏 8 月、畿内周辺の領主を入れ替えた。弟の秀長は、それまでの紀伊（和歌山県）や和泉（大阪府南西部）に加えて大和（奈良県）をあたえられ、大和郡山城（奈良県大和郡山市）を居城に定めた。このとき甥の秀次も近江（滋賀県）をあたえられ、八幡山城（近江八幡市）を築いた。

それは秀次の居城であり、同時に豊臣政権の近江における拠点でもあった。東に 6 キロほどのところにある安土城は、織田信長のイメージが強すぎるゆえに、秀吉は利用したくなかったのである。城は標高 272 メートルの八幡山（鶴翼山）山頂の山城と、標高 130 ～ 90 メートルの南側山腹から山麓にかけての居館からなる。戦国時代を思わせる二元構造なのは、前年に小牧・長久手合戦があったばかりで、まだ徳川家康も臣従していないという軍事的緊張感の表れかもしれない。

山頂まではロープウェーを使えば 3 分で着く。そこには累々たる総石垣の城が展開しており、豊臣政権の圧倒的な力が感じられる。

山頂駅の正面が二の丸で、山頂展望館への階段を設置するために石垣が崩されているなど残念な面もあるが、東南方向に折れがつけられながら、壮大な規模の石垣で完全に囲まれている。

ここから北西に向かって城が展開し、本丸を中心に、北に北の丸、西に西の丸、その南に少し離れて出丸が放射状に配置されている。本丸までは何度も屈曲するように虎口がもうけられ、本丸入口は本丸内に食い込んだ内枡形になっている。

本丸は昭和 36 年（ 1961 ）から秀次の菩提寺である瑞龍寺の敷地になっており、移転に先立って行われた発掘調査では、礎石や金箔瓦を含む瓦などが出土したという。

樹木伐採で味わえる天正年間の石垣のスケール

高石垣で囲まれた本丸は、南西や北端などで塁線が何度も複雑に曲げられ、各所で横矢が掛けられるよう厳重に構築されている。狭い山上の地形を活かしながら、徹底した防御態勢が敷かれていたのがわかる。

八幡山城の石垣は自然石と割石が併用され、天正年間の石垣らしい野面積みで積まれているが、本丸の南西角などに、矢穴で割られた長めの直方体の石による算木積みなど、あたらしい技法も見られる。これは天正 18 年（ 1590 ）、小田原征伐後に秀次が尾張（愛知県西部）の清洲城（愛知県清須市）に移った後、城主になった京極高次が手を加えたものだと思われる。

石垣の石材は主に八幡山で採れる湖東流紋岩が使われているが、秀次時代の石垣にはこの時代の例に漏れず、宝篋印塔などの転用石も見られる。

本丸の周りに配置された北の丸や西の丸からは、眺望もすばらしい。北の丸からは安土城はもとより遠く伊吹山まで、西の丸からは琵琶湖方面が一望のもとで、この場所の地の利の良さがうかがえる。また、北の丸の北方の尾根には石垣の先が堀切で遮断されているなど、やはり防御には抜かりがない。

ところで、北の丸は周囲の樹木や篠竹などが伐採され、展望が確保されたうえ石垣がよく見える。麓からでも眺められるが、これは「八幡山の景観を良くする会」が 2017 年以降、ボランティアで伐採に取り組んできた成果である。

出丸の周囲はさらによく伐採され、天正 13 年（ 1585 ）の築城時に山上に積まれた圧巻の石垣を、間近でしっかりと観察できる。

安土城譲りの圧倒的な求心的構造

山腹から山麓の居館も圧巻である。山麓からまっすぐに大手道が続き、その両側には重臣たちが屋敷を構えた平坦地が、石垣で階段状に造成され、道の突き当りには内枡形の巨大な虎口がある。そこには長辺が 1.5 メートル程度の巨石が鏡石としていくつも積まれ、訪れた人を威圧する。ちなみに、居館の周辺も前述のボランティアの手で、木々の伐採が進められている。

直線で登っていく大手道と、その先の厳重な虎口。これは安土城の構造と同じである。虎口の前までは楽に往来でき、虎口から先の城主の居館は、その下と切り離して厳重に守られている。こうして強いヒエラルキーが視覚的にも表現される。信長が安土城で実現した圧倒的に求心的な構造。安土城は廃しながらも、秀次と背後にいる秀吉は、この信長の発想を八幡山城に取り入れたのである。

平成 12 年（ 2000 ）から行われた調査で、礎石や石組の溝のほか、金箔瓦や飾り瓦なども大量に出土した。その際、この居館が人為的に埋められた痕があったという。

文禄 4 年（ 1595 ）に前城主の秀次が切腹し、妻子らが惨殺される秀次事件が起きたのち、城主の京極高次は大津城に移され、八幡山城は廃城になった。謀反を起こしたというレッテルを貼られた秀次とともに、この城も誕生してわずか 10 年で記憶から消し去られたのである。

圧倒的なスケールの石垣を前にして、その上を飾っていた往時の絢爛豪華な建造物を頭に思い描くと、秀次事件の痛ましさと異常さが強く感じられてくる。

山麓の家臣たちの屋敷地は水堀で囲まれていた。堀は防御に貢献すると同時に、琵琶湖とつながって水運を支えていた。この堀の外側には、安土から移住させた商人たちの町が碁盤の目のように整えられ、廃城後も近江商人の町として栄え、この堀の水運も活かしながら多くの豪商が輩出した。

この堀はいまも城下の近江八幡を代表する景観として残り、豪商たちを生んだ町並みは伝統的建造物群保存地域として、往時の面影をたもっている。

article_text:
È morto all’età di 84 anni Rudi Fuchs , storico dell’arte, curatore e direttore museale tra le figure più influenti del sistema europeo dell’arte contemporanea del secondo Novecento. Nato a Eindhoven il 28 aprile 1942, Fuchs aveva diretto alcune delle principali istituzioni museali europee, dal Van Abbemuseum di Eindhoven allo Stedelijk Museum di Amsterdam, passando per il Gemeentemuseum dell’Aia e, in Italia, per il Castello di Rivoli , di cui fu il primo direttore.

La sua carriera è stata segnata da un modo di intendere il progetto espositivo fondato soprattutto sulle opere e sulle relazioni che queste potevano stabilire tra loro. Accostamenti, contrasti e affinità prendevano spesso il posto di un impianto teorico rigido, lasciando al pubblico un maggiore spazio di interpretazione.

Dal Van Abbemuseum a documenta 7

Fuchs studiò storia dell’arte all’Università di Leida e nel 1975, a 33 anni, divenne direttore del Van Abbemuseum di Eindhoven, risultando all’epoca il più giovane direttore museale dei Paesi Bassi. Durante il suo mandato spostò l’attenzione dell’istituzione verso l’arte contemporanea europea, con un interesse particolare per le ricerche sviluppate in Germania, Austria e Italia.

La consacrazione internazionale arrivò nel 1982, quando fu direttore artistico di documenta 7 a Kassel. L’edizione riunì 182 artisti – tra cui Joseph Beuys , per la leggendaria azione delle 7000 querce – segnò una presa di posizione rispetto alle precedenti impostazioni della manifestazione. Fuchs rinunciò infatti a un titolo e a un tema generale, privilegiando l’autonomia delle opere e le relazioni visive costruite nello spazio.

Il suo approccio curatoriale procedeva frequentemente per accostamenti tra artisti appartenenti a contesti e generazioni differenti, senza imporre al visitatore una lettura univoca. Una metodologia che avrebbe attraversato anche le successive esperienze museali.

Rudi Fuchs, primo direttore del Castello di Rivoli

Nel 1984 Fuchs fu chiamato in Piemonte per contribuire alla nascita del Castello di Rivoli Museo d’Arte Contemporanea, diventandone il primo direttore. Rimase alla guida dell’istituzione fino al 1991, accompagnandone i primi anni di costruzione dell’identità museale. Il Castello aprì al pubblico il 19 dicembre 1984 con Ouverture , mostra inaugurale curata dallo stesso Fuchs e pensata non semplicemente come esposizione temporanea, ma anche come possibile punto di partenza per la futura collezione permanente.

Il progetto riuniva circa 70 artisti internazionali e metteva in dialogo protagonisti dell’Arte Povera come Alighiero Boetti , Jannis Kounellis , Mario Merz , Marisa Merz , Michelangelo Pistoletto e Gilberto Zorio con artisti legati alle ricerche minimaliste e concettuali europee e americane. Tra questi figuravano Carl Andre , Donald Judd , Bruce Nauman , Sol LeWitt e Daniel Buren .

Fuchs contribuì così a definire fin dall’inizio Rivoli come un museo internazionale, nel quale l’esperienza italiana dell’Arte Povera poteva essere riletta all’interno di una rete più ampia di relazioni con le ricerche europee e statunitensi. Centrale era anche il rapporto diretto degli artisti con l’architettura del Castello, con opere e interventi concepiti specificamente per gli ambienti dell’edificio.

Nel 2024, a quarant’anni dall’apertura, il museo aveva richiamato esplicitamente quell’esperienza con Ouverture 2024 , riallestimento della collezione costruito anche come omaggio alla mostra inaugurale ideata da Fuchs.

Dal Gemeentemuseum allo Stedelijk Museum

Mentre proseguiva l’esperienza italiana, nel 1987 Fuchs assunse anche la direzione del Gemeentemuseum dell’Aia, oggi Kunstmuseum Den Haag, dove rimase fino al 1993.

Nel febbraio dello stesso anno passò alla guida dello Stedelijk Museum di Amsterdam, prima come direttore generale e successivamente come direttore artistico. Rimase nell’istituzione fino al 1° gennaio 2003, continuando a sviluppare una pratica espositiva basata sulla possibilità di mettere in relazione opere provenienti da epoche e contesti diversi. Tornò allo Stedelijk nel 2016 come guest curator della mostra Excitement , una ricognizione sull’arte degli ultimi cinquant’anni costruita a partire dalle collezioni dello Stedelijk, del Van Abbemuseum e del Gemeentemuseum.

Accanto alla direzione museale, Fuchs svolse attività di insegnamento all’Università di Amsterdam e continuò a lavorare come critico e autore indipendente, pubblicando numerosi saggi e testi sull’arte contemporanea. Dal 2009 al 2022 firmò inoltre una rubrica settimanale per De Groene Amsterdammer .

Nel corso della carriera ricevette numerosi riconoscimenti internazionali. Nel 1998 fu nominato Commendatore dell’Ordine al Merito della Repubblica Italiana, a testimonianza anche del rapporto costruito con il sistema artistico del Paese a partire dall’esperienza di Rivoli.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 以下是艺术圈人士喜欢——或应该喜欢——的35家餐厅。

There is no real reason for dealers and collectors to return to the same hokey fondue spot in Basel every year, or the same mildewed dive bar on Miami Beach, but they do, driven perhaps by the promise of friendly faces and easy familiarity. There are memories in these places."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As I discussed on the Artnet News podcast The Art Angle with Artnet’s editor in chief, Andrew Russeth , fine art professionals wind up eating at a handful of very intentionally chosen places. A disclaimer: It is by no means comprehensive, and it is largely subjective, grounded in our own circles, interests, and years on the ground in the industry."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Some selections are obvious. This year saw the opening of four restaurants attached to big-name art institutions in New York: Marcel (in the basement of Sotheby’s ), Zoli (attached to Amant ), Symone ( MoMA PS1 ), and Oberon ( New Museum ). The city has also recently welcomed a handful of restaurants that are independent of any art space but that are known for their art collections ( Humm in the West Village, Oriana in Little Italy) or their art ties ( Cavalier , which is operated by artist Yasmin Kaytmaz and dealer Alex Adler )."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Other selections are less obvious, like a gourmet grocery store positioned at the nexus of the Tribeca gallery scene, or an unassuming tavern where dealers on the Upper East Side can still get a burger for under $20. It feels good to be at Sotheby’s in the basement of Marcel Breuer ’s building. The luxe French food? The prices are formidable ($176 for a whole Dover sole, $22 for a side of fries), and the execution is oddly wan. But you are here for other reasons. —Andrew Russeth"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Oberon"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The recently expanded New Museum came with a splashy restaurant from the Oberon Group , Henry Rich ’s restaurant company, whose portfolio includes Rhodora , Rucola , June , and Anaïs . The menu veers toward the approachable, but the design of Oberon is where the creativity lives: You approach through a silvery chute in Freeman Alley, and enter an OMA -designed room that looks like a spaceship made entirely of cork, lit by an interactive Ian Cheng piece behind the bar. Photo: Andrew Russeth"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Because they opened within a few weeks of each other this past spring, Zoli, the restaurant at Lonti Ebers ‘s Bushwick art complex Amant , is often compared to Marcel , the new restaurant at the Sotheby’s Breuer Building flagship. Take a bite of whatever fish chef Ned Baldwin sourced that week (tilefish, the last time I visited, though as I write this, I see sanddab on the menu) while gazing at Pierre Huyghe ’s sludgy, post-nuclear fish tanks, the centerpiece of the dining room, with genetically modified noxious-green fish drifting within. (Tell me that pairing doesn’t provoke your palate!) Up next is DeVonn Charles Francis , who is bringing French-Caribbean cuisine to campus this fall. This is Francis’s first restaurant, and he arrives with experience running his own catering business, Yardy World , and previously managing the flowers at Ignacio Mattos ’s late-lamented Flora Bar at the Breuer Building , back when it was the Met Breuer . Chef Aiden O’Neal , who ran M. I recommend having a roast chicken and a glass of ice-cold aquavit. —A.A.", "links": [{"text": "was an investor", "url": "https://caper.media/p/ned-baldwin-houseman-joan-jonas-drawing"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Cavalier"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Georgia-Gardner-Gray-at-Cavalier-1024x576.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A work by Georgia Gardner Gray at Cavalier.
